lessons.title: Moat Trend: Is the Advantage Widening, Stable, or Narrowing?

body.text: Two questions, not one. How strong is the moat, and which way is it moving? Most investors answer the first and are surprised by the second.

children.text: Chapter 5 gave you a scorecard that measures a moat at a point in time. Chapters 6.1 to 6.3 covered the three forces that erode it. This lesson combines them into the question that actually drives returns from here: is this advantage getting stronger or weaker? A wide moat that is narrowing can be a worse investment than a narrow moat that is widening, particularly once valuation is considered.
Level and Direction Are Different Things

body.title: Illustrative: Moat Scorecard Totals Over Five Years (out of 24)

children.text: In year 1, Company A scores 21 out of 24 and Company B scores 12. Any screen for quality picks A. By year 5, A has fallen to 15 and B has risen to 18, and they have swapped places. An investor who bought A in year 1 at a premium multiple paid for a moat that was already weakening. An investor who noticed B improving bought an advantage the market had not yet recognised.

body.text: Share prices tend to reflect the current moat, because that is what the last decade of financials shows. What they reflect poorly is the direction of travel, because that shows up in operating detail long before it reaches reported returns. The direction is where an attentive retail investor has a genuine edge over a screen.

children.text: The Signals, Sorted by How Early They Appear

body.caption: Leading and lagging indicators of moat direction
headers: What a Narrowing Moat Looks Like

cells: Earliest
Volume versus price split in results presentations
Growth increasingly comes from price while volumes stagnate or fall
Early
Incremental ROCE versus reported ROCE
New capital earns materially less than the existing business
Early
Share in the fastest-growing channel or segment
The company leads in the shrinking channel and lags in the growing one
Early
Customer concentration and contract terms
Top customers take a larger share of revenue, or renewals come with discounts
Middle
Advertising and promotion, or customer acquisition spend
Rising as a percentage of revenue simply to hold position
Middle
Gross margin drift
A slow decline of half a point a year, easy to dismiss quarter by quarter
Lagging
Reported ROCE and market share
By the time these clearly decline, the erosion has been under way for years

body.title: Measure the Gap
body.prompt: A company reports a five-year average ROCE of 24%, but its five-year incremental ROCE works out to 12%. What is the gap, in percentage points?
body.explanation: 24% − 12% = 12 percentage points. A gap this wide means new capital earns half what old capital earns, so the reported average will keep falling as new investment becomes a larger share of the total. This single comparison is the most useful early warning of a narrowing moat.

body.title: Direction of travel, in observable terms

columns.label: Widening
points: Market share gains without cutting prices
Incremental ROCE at or above the historical level
Switching costs deepening as customers use more of the product
Network getting denser, improving service and cost per unit
A second moat source being added to the first

columns.label: Narrowing
points: Share held only through discounts or higher trade schemes
Incremental ROCE well below reported ROCE
New entrants funded by patient capital
Regulatory consultation aimed at the company's pricing
Capex concentrated in the legacy technology or channel

children.text: The most reliable single sign of widening is gaining share while holding or raising prices. Almost anything else can be bought. Winning customers from rivals without paying for them is the behaviour that only a strengthening advantage produces.

body.caption: Four combinations and what each means for an investor

cells: Wide moat
The best case, and usually the most expensive. Justifies a premium multiple if the runway is real
The most dangerous case. Historical numbers look superb, the multiple is high, and returns are quietly declining
Narrow moat
Often the best risk-adjusted opportunity. The market prices the current moat, not the improving one
Avoid. Limited protection and weakening further, with no margin for error

body.label: The combination to fear most
body.value: Wide moat, narrowing trend, premium valuation
body.context: Every backward-looking number supports the thesis while the forward-looking ones do not. This is how quality investors lose money on quality companies.

children.text: track three or four leading indicators only, such as the volume and price split, any discounting mentioned in the concall, and customer or channel commentary. This takes about twenty minutes per company.
run the full twelve-criterion scorecard after the annual report, and compare with the previous year's score and reasons.
rescore immediately after a regulatory consultation, a large acquisition, a new well-funded entrant, or a technology announcement that changes the industry.
Write down the score and the reasons, not just the conclusion. A year later, the reasons are what let you see whether your thesis is intact or you have been quietly moving the goalposts.

body.title: Read the Direction
body.question: A company's reported ROCE has been steady at 26% for three years. Over the same period, volumes have been flat while realisations rose 8% a year, trade discounts have increased, and its share in e-commerce channels is well below its share in traditional retail. What is the most likely moat trend?
options: Widening, since ROCE is holding up
Stable, since nothing has declined yet
Narrowing, because growth is entirely price-led, discounts are rising, and the company is weak in the growing channel
Impossible to judge without five more years of data
body.explanation: Steady ROCE is the lagging indicator. Every leading indicator points the other way: no volume growth, growth bought through price, rising discounts, and a weak position where the market is shifting. This is the classic profile of a moat that will show decline in reported numbers two or three years from now.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: The most reliable single sign of a widening moat is gaining market share without cutting ___.
body.explanation: Share can always be bought with discounts. Share won while holding or raising prices is evidence that the advantage itself is strengthening.

body.title: Two Stocks, One Slot in the Portfolio
body.scenario: Company G is a dominant listed consumer business: scorecard 20 of 24, ROCE 31%, trading at 62 times earnings. Its volumes have been flat for two years, price-led growth is around 7%, and a well-funded rival has entered its main category. Company H is a mid cap industrial: scorecard 14 of 24, ROCE 19% rising from 13% five years ago, incremental ROCE of 24%, trading at 24 times earnings. It has gained share for three consecutive years without discounting, and two smaller competitors have exited.
body.prompt: Which offers better prospects from here, and what could prove you wrong in each case?
body.modelAnswer: Company H looks better on the combination of trend and price. Its incremental ROCE of 24% exceeds its reported 19%, which means new capital earns more than old, the signature of a widening moat. Share gains without discounting and competitor exits support that, and at 24 times earnings the market is still pricing the historical, weaker business. Company G has the stronger moat today, but the leading indicators are poor: flat volumes, price-led growth, and a new funded competitor, all while the multiple assumes the advantage is secure. That is the dangerous quadrant. What would prove me wrong: for H, the share gains may reflect a cyclical upturn rather than a structural advantage, so if incremental ROCE falls back towards 13% or the exited competitors return when conditions improve, the widening was an illusion; its scorecard weakness also means less protection if it stumbles. For G, if volume growth returns once the category recovers and the rival fails to gain traction, then the flat volumes were temporary and the moat is intact, in which case 62 times earnings may still prove acceptable over a long horizon, as Chapter 1 showed. The practical answer is that G needs a lower entry price to be attractive, while H needs its trend to be confirmed for two more years.

body.title: Set Up Your Moat Trend Tracker
steps: For each holding, record today's scorecard total and the three weakest criteria
Pick four leading indicators to track quarterly, including the volume and price split and any discounting commentary
Note the current incremental ROCE and reported ROCE, and the gap between them
After each quarterly result, update the indicators and write one line on whether the moat widened, held, or narrowed
Rescore the full scorecard once a year and compare it with the previous year, reasons included
Decide in advance what score or indicator change would make you reduce the position

body.text: Companies A, B, G, and H are hypothetical illustrations. Nothing here is an investment recommendation.

points: A moat has two dimensions: how strong it is today, and which direction it is moving
Share prices usually reflect the current moat but not the trend, which is where an attentive investor has an edge
Leading indicators include the volume and price split, incremental ROCE, share in the growing channel, and customer concentration
Reported ROCE and market share are lagging indicators, confirming erosion years after it began
The most reliable sign of widening is gaining share without cutting prices
Wide moat plus narrowing trend plus a premium multiple is the most dangerous combination in quality investing
